newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Sweden, European royalty mourn Prince Bertil.
newsitem.headline: Sweden, European royalty mourn Prince Bertil.

text.p: Church bells rang out across Stockholm on Monday to bid farewell to Sweden's Prince Bertil, whose secret 33-year romance with a British actress became the country's best known love story.

Tributes flooded in for the popular prince while 600 guests, including representatives from all European royal families, gathered in the capital to attend Sweden's first royal funeral since King Gustaf VI Adolf's death in 1973.
The guests included Britain's Prince Philip, Denmark's Queen Margrethe, Norway's King Harald, Spain's Princess Christina, and Princess Margriet of the Netherlands.
Prince Bertil, who was the uncle of reigning King Carl XVI Gustaf, died in his sleep at his Stockholm home eight days ago, aged 84, after ailing for several years.
His wife, Welsh-born Princess Lilian, who he finally married in 1976, was by his side when he died.

"His contributions over many years to the worlds of industry and sports, as well as his uncommon ability to touch people's lives, will be fondly remembered," said a condolence message from U.S. President Bill Clinton.
"He was a fine example of Sweden's best and will surely be missed by all who know -- or knew of -- him."
The day of mourning began with church bells across Stockholm ringing for 30 minutes as daylight broke at 0700 GMT.
The city ground to a halt at midday as guests attended a funeral service at the palace chapel in central Stockholm.
To the strains of Johann Sebastian Bach's Prelude in E-minor, Princess Lilian walked into the chapel, accompanied by King Carl XVI Gustaf and Queen Sylvia.
After the service, up to 100,000 people lined the city streets to watch the funeral procession surrounding the prince's coffin, draped in Sweden's blue and yellow flag.
To the beat of a single drum, a procession of about 1,000 police and soldiers, on horseback and wearing white fur, military hats, wound its way out of the city to the royal graveyard at Haga.
The relationship of Prince Bertil, the third-born son of King Gustav VI Adolf, and divorcee Lilian Craig has become a modern day love story in Sweden.

After meeting and falling in love in London during World War Two, the pair were forced to keep their relationship secret for 33 years for the sake of the Swedish crown and to forestall a constitutional crisis.
Prince Bertil's elder brother and heir to the throne, Prince Gustaf Adolf, had died in a plane crash in 1947 while the next brother, Sigvard, waived his right to the throne by marrying a commoner.
This put Prince Bertil next in line until his infant nephew, Crown Prince Carl Gustaf, the infant son of Prince Gustaf Adolf, came of age.

If Prince Bertil had married a commoner he would have had to renounce his right to the throne. This could have meant the throne falling vacant, raising the prospect of a republic, if the king died before the crown prince came of age.

It was not until after the crown prince became king in 1973, and married a few years later, that Prince Bertil and his clandestine partner of 33 years, Lilian, finally married and appeared together in public.
